extracted.intended_audience: administrative lawyers, regulatory professionals, agency counsel, and policy stakeholders interested in APA notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether an agency's final rule satisfies the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements—particularly whether the final rule is a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule and whether the agency adequately responded to comments and explained changes in position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth / in character with original scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, an agency may revise a final rule after initial notice only if the changes 'are in character with the original scheme' and the final rule is a 'logical outgrowth' of the notice and comments from the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court applied this standard to hold the Final Rule invalid because its changes (e.g., eliminating the Final Sodium Target and abandoning the whole-grain requirement) were not in character with the Interim Final Rule. This dimension asks whether the final regulatory text reasonably follows from what was proposed such that interested parties could have anticipated and commented on the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of notice to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule must enable the public 'to discern what [is] at stake.' If the final rule 'substantially departs from the terms or substance of the proposed rule,' the notice is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the notice (proposed or interim final rule) gave fair warning of the substance of the changes later adopted. Example from the case: the Interim Final Rule focused on delaying compliance requirements and did not discuss abandoning sodium targets; thus the Final Rule's elimination of the Final Sodium Target was not a logical outgrowth and notice was inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with federal law (Chevron analysis/deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the final rule is consistent with relevant federal statutes can be measured using Chevron deference: if statutes do not unambiguously resolve the issue, the agency's permissible construction is entitled to substantial deference under Chevron step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court here applied Chevron and found the statutes did not unambiguously support either party’s interpretation, so it deferred to USDA’s permissible construction. This criterion evaluates statutory interpretation and whether deference to agency expertise is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unexplained or arbitrary decisionmaking (arbitrary-and-capricious review)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rule must not reflect unexplained and arbitrary decisionmaking; agencies must provide reasoned explanation for their choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges claiming arbitrary and capricious action require the agency to articulate a rational connection between facts and choices. The plaintiff alleged unexplained and arbitrary decisionmaking; the Court addressed but ultimately found other procedural failings determinative in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unacknowledged or unexplained change in position
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may not silently change course: significant shifts from prior positions must be acknowledged and explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasized that where an agency 'completely changes its position between the Interim and Final Rules,' deference does not excuse failure to provide sufficient notice and explanation. Example: moving from retaining 100% whole-grain requirement with limited exemptions to abandoning the requirement entirely without adequate explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate and adequate response to public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must appropriately respond to public comments submitted on the proposed rule; failure to do so can render the rule procedurally defective under the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff alleged USDA did not appropriately respond to comments; the logical-outgrowth/notice inquiry overlaps with whether comments were considered and whether the final rule addresses concerns raised. Assessors should look for record citations showing reasoned reply to material comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on adopting changes that go beyond the proposed scope (substantial departure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rule cannot 'substantially depart' from the terms or substance of the proposed rule; such departures render notice inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: the Interim Final Rule delayed compliance but did not discuss elimination of sodium targets; the Final Rule eliminated the Final Sodium Target and converted a limited, case-by-case exemption for whole grains into wholesale abandonment. These are paradigmatic 'substantial departures' that fail the logical-outgrowth test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural obligations remain despite deference in complex technical programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where courts give agencies substantial deference on technical or policy matters, agencies still must satisfy APA procedural requirements (adequate notice, explanation, and response to comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that 'extremely considerable deference is provided' in complex technical regulatory programs, but 'that deference does not absolve the agency of the necessary requirements under the APA to provide sufficient notice of the Final Rule.' Evaluations should therefore not excuse procedural lapses simply because the subject matter is technical.
